summary:
Tatarstan stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that includes anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days, and deportation.

Same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are prohibited, trans-specific healthcare has been effectively banned since 2023, and no discrimination protection exists. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records at least 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024.

Human Rights Watch reported 101 extremism-related convictions by 30 June 2025 for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or display of its symbols, comprising 98 administrative and 3 criminal cases. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation, two sentenced to prison and seventeen pending or unknown.

On 15 May 2025, three staff of two publishing houses were charged with running an extremist organisation under article 282.2 and face up to 12 years in prison. Repeated display of banned symbols is punishable by up to four years in prison.

The UK Home Office note places the elevated state-persecution exception, which covers trans people, public LGBT+ advocates and North Caucasus residents likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, outside ordinary regions such as Tatarstan.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement volume has grown alongside severity: Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines bringing more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget over two years.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented when, within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling in January 2024, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars; about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tatarstan face the same national prohibitions as elsewhere in Russia: no legal gender recognition, no gender-affirming care since 2023, no same-sex marriage, and no discrimination protection.

Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia, and the UK Home Office recognises LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, as a particular social group under the refugee convention.

Physical coercion against trans people is documented: BBC Russian (27 July 2024) reported on a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping.

In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Tatarstan's regional authorities have issued republic-specific directives on enforcement of the national extremism or propaganda provisions is not sourced in the available inventory.

The current summary's claim that at least 139 people were impacted between 2022 and 2024 is attributed to the June 2025 UK Home Office note; the underlying breakdown by region, including any Tatarstan-specific figure, is not resolved in the sources provided.

No Tatarstan-specific incident of a trans person facing extremism charges, raid, or detention is documented in the inventory; enforcement data is national.
